summary:
This L0009 run was started by the line's timer, not by an instruction. It had no 'Asked' items, so the empty answers list is right. It made no claims and registered no experiments. It answered my open point from the previous review and added the event loop's hand-off to moving stacks, on branch method/rest at c6ad1ff. Stacks are still run only offline.

Everything I reran reproduced in a fresh clone of c6ad1ff. The method tests gave 55 passed. The program's frozen engine tests (referee/tests), run against the branch with the method off, gave 74 passed. The three stall layers (seed 1 at f* 0.3, seed 2 at f* 0.3, seed 1 at f* 0.4; Gamma 2, depth 5) gave the same event times, sphere pairs, slips, mode changes, stack durations (0.398, 0.915 and 0.953 time units), friction losses and books residuals as evidence/L0009-build-2026-11-25-4.json, bit for bit. Only the CPU seconds differed.

My previous challenge is answered and the fix acted. That challenge was that a contact labelled rolling but slipping was held at constant slip with friction work booked on it. Decision D0084 now starts any rolling contact with slip above 1e-13 sliding. In the stall pair both contacts switch (the plate contact slipped 0.0171, the top contact 0.0421). The plate contact slides for 0.0038 time units, then rolls. So the output differs from the old code from the first step. To check the physics rather than the books, I evaluated every accepted integrator step of five stacks: the three above plus two neighbours, seed 3 at f* 0.3 and seed 2 at f* 0.4. In none did friction ever add energy beyond round-off (largest 1.4e-14). In none did a contact marked rolling slip by more than 4e-14. All pushes stayed positive (smallest 0.014). Positive friction power does appear inside rejected trial steps and bisection probes past an event, but never in an accepted state. That is expected and harmless.

The hand-off's booking (D0085) is right. I checked the algebra: in the rider's frame the upper sphere loses one half m vn squared, and the rest of its lab-frame change is the plate's work through the rider. The residuals in the evidence (1e-17 or smaller) confirm it. This also settles my earlier smaller point, that the replay removed the residual approach outside the books: the event-loop path now books it.

At neighbouring conditions the behaviour is the same. Seed 3 at f* 0.3 stalls at local time 5.650. Both its contacts start sliding, and the stack runs 0.79 time units, books 2e-14. Seed 2 at f* 0.4 stalls at 4.480. Both contacts slide, and the stack runs 1.11 time units, books 3e-13. Seed 1 at f* 0.5 finishes its first cycle with no stack event.

One caveat matters for the next stage and for the cost question to Chris. The durations of 0.4 to 0.95 time units are how long the isolated pair lasts. They are not how long a stack would last in the layer. I moved every other free sphere along its free-flight path from the event state and asked when it would first touch one of the two stack spheres. This ignores their own collisions, so it is a rough proxy. In all three stall layers some sphere reaches the stack within 0.002 to 0.03 time units, one to eight percent of the offline duration. Two to four spheres do so before the stack ends. Once stacks are fed back, they will be interrupted or grow long before the top sphere slides off. So the 7 to 15 seconds of Python per offline stack is not the cost per stack in a layer. The number of stack rebuilds per cycle will decide that. The line's state ('each stack, run offline, moved for 0.40 to 0.95 time units until its top sphere left') is literally true and says 'offline'. It should not be read as a stack lifetime.

One small wording point. The question to Chris says each first stall 'takes 125 or more integrator steps'. Only the replay's 125 steps are in the evidence. My count of accepted steps in the three event-loop stacks is about 115 to 146, so 'over a hundred' is what the evidence supports.

The lines.jsonl note and state for L0009 match the evidence otherwise. program check passes apart from my own scratch, which I removed. The latest approval is from 2026-11-24 03:19 UTC, more than a day old. The question to Chris (does an integrated moving stack count as time-stepping?) is still open, asked for the fourth time, and honestly framed.

run_conditions.assessment: The run started at 11:42:28 UTC, 28 seconds after its scheduled time. Its final commit is stamped 12:06:50 UTC, which matches the recorded end, so the end time is now measured rather than forecast. The run took about 25 minutes, well within its limit. Ten minutes of that were lost waiting on checks launched through a tool this Linux worker does not have. The summary records this as an interruption. My reruns of its checks took 37 to 80 seconds for the test suites and 7 to 20 seconds of CPU per stack, so the recorded 0.12 CPU hours is plausible. It is a sum of timings measured inside the scripts, and the summary says so. No jobs are in flight (active.jsonl is empty). The scratch folder is empty. The data folder is 685 megabytes of the 15 gigabytes allowed, with 90 gigabytes free against a floor of 40. I found no files written outside the program's folders in the run's window, and no new pytest folders under ~/.tmp since 09:46. The machine did not limit the science. Waiting are stage four, feeding stacks back into the event loop (the next timer run), and Chris's answer to the time-stepping question.
discrepancies: The question to Chris cites '125 or more integrator steps' per first-stall stack. Only the offline replay's 125 is recorded. The three event-loop stacks' step counts are not in the evidence, and by my count one has about 115 accepted steps.
Fixed since last review: the recorded end time (12:06:50Z) matches the final commit, rather than being a forecast.
